newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's Riksbank wants to keep currency policies.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's Riksbank wants to keep currency policies.

text.p: Sweden's central bank governor, Urban Backstrom, on Thursday stressed the importance of turning down an Exchange Rate Competence Inquiry's proposal to transfer the responsibility for exchange rate policy decisions from the Riksbank.

"The investigator seems to have overlooked the fact that monetary policy and exchange rate policy are two sides of the same coin," Backstrom said in a speech released before he was due to deliver it in Gothenburg, southern Sweden, on Thursday night.
"The problem with the report's proposal is that it would be more difficult to make permanent price stability credible.
"The proposal accordingly counters other legislative proposals concerning the Riksbank that are being discussed. It is therefore important that the investigator's proposal be rejected."
Possible new laws aim to increase confidence in the economic policies and thereby contribute to greater stability both in the economic and financial markets, Backstrom said.
He said there was now a lot positive with the country's economy, pointing to growth picking up, a large trade surplus and very low inflation.
In its quarterly inflation report, which the Riksbank presented earlier on Thursday, the bank lowered its inflation forecasts to 0.5 percent for 1997 and somewhat below two percent for 1998.
The Riksbank's target is inflation of two percent with an allowed deviation of one percentage point on either side.
"The Swedish economy displays many favourable features," Backstrom said.
"We are gradually extricating ourselves from several decades of recurrent economic problems that culminated in a profound crisis in the early 1990s," he said.

"Provided Sweden continues to implement disciplined budget and monetary policies and generally enhances confidence in economic policy, there are good indications that, after the slowdown in 1996, growth will become successively stronger again without generating higher inflation."
But on the negative side, Backstrom noted that unemployment was high, running at 8.8 percent in February.
"Even if wage formation does adapt sooner or later to the currently low inflation, it is disquieting that this is taking so long," Backstrom said.
"Most of the evidence suggests that unemployment's equilibrium level has risen, which means that if nothing is done, unemployment is liable to remain high though (economic) activity improves."
If unemployment's equilibrium level has risen, something should be done to bring it down, Backstrom said, but added that this was out of bounds for monetary and demand policy.
